title: Mahajanaka's swim
hookLine: shipwrecked, he swims seven days without seeing land, because effort is never wasted
last: TEMIYA — SILENCE CAN BE A CHOICE.

lines: A PROJECT WITH NO SHORE IN SIGHT.
cards: A thesis in its third version. A recovery that moves an inch a week. A job hunt on its fortieth application.
Some projects have no shore in sight, and at some point a reasonable voice asks: what's the point? You can't even see the end.
Today's story, the second of the ten long Jatakas, asks that question in the middle of the ocean. A prince, a sinking ship, and a goddess who wants to know why he's still swimming.

teach.b: Mahajanaka is a prince born in exile. His father, the king of Mithila, was killed by his own brother, and his mother fled while pregnant.
When the boy grows up and learns the truth, he decides to win back what was lost, so he joins a trading ship bound for a far country to make his fortune.
Out at sea, the ship breaks apart. The others weep and pray and drown. Mahajanaka, the story says, does something practical.
He eats his fill, soaks his clothes in oil against the cold water, climbs the mast, and leaps as far out as he can, clear of the wreck and the sea creatures. Then he swims.

teach.h: SEVEN DAYS, NO LAND IN SIGHT.
teach.b: Seven days, the story says, with no land in sight.
On the seventh day a sea goddess named Manimekhala appears above the waves and asks him, in effect: why bother? There's no shore. You'll die out here.

His answer is the heart of the story. A person who makes the effort, even if they die trying, is free from blame, he says, and giving up guarantees failure, while effort at least gives a chance. Effort is never wasted.

Moved by his answer, she lifts him out of the sea and carries him to Mithila, where, in time, he becomes king. In the tradition, this life shows the perfection of viriya: effort, energy, courage that keeps going.
Not effort because success is certain. Effort because it's the only part that's yours.

how: Buddhists tell the Mahajanaka story as an example of viriya, effort, and in Theravada countries such as Thailand it is retold in books, art and temple murals.

o: a swim that ends once the shore comes into view
effort that keeps going with no shore in sight
a prayer that brings a goddess to the rescue

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: swam seven days with no land in sight
the sea goddess who asked why

s: Mahajanaka swam because he could see the shore
for seven days there was no land in sight. he swam anyway.
he ate, oiled his clothes, climbed the mast, and leapt clear of the wreck.
the goddess rescued him because he prayed to her
she was moved by his answer: effort is never wasted.

games.q: you've swum for seven days. a goddess appears and says there's no shore: why bother? what do you say?
o: effort is never wasted, even if I die trying.
games.why: he defends his effort, and she's so moved that she carries him to Mithila, where he later becomes king.

practice: Let your breathing find its rhythm, like a steady stroke, and bring up one thing you're working on where you can't see the end, the tiredness and the why-bother voice included.
With each out-breath, picture one stroke: not the shore, just this stroke, then the next. When your mind drifts, coming back is its own kind of stroke.

wordCard.voice: Mahajanaka's swim. Seven days in the open sea, because effort is never wasted.

orig.note: Pali: effort, energy; the perfection the tradition links with Mahajanaka's life.

carryVoice: Your line: swim anyway. Seven days, and not once did he see land. Ninety-five, and still swimming.
